text: Intervention White/pink noise during focused tasks (auditory, ambient). Optional ambient white or pink noise played during attention-demanding tasks, user-adjustable volume, off by default for users without elevated ADHD traits. Expected effect: Small improvement in laboratory attention/executive task performance in ADHD or high-symptom youth (g = 0.249, 95% CI 0.135–0.363); small impairment in non-ADHD individuals (g = −0.212, 95% CI −0.355 to −0.069, k = 11) (Nigg et al. 2024). Evidence (meta-analysis): A preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis (13 studies, 335 participants) found white/pink noise gave a small benefit on laboratory attention tasks in youth with ADHD or elevated attention problems. The same noise impaired performance in non-ADHD comparison participants. No brown-noise studies existed and evidence is lab-based, not real-world. Contraindications: users without ADHD traits (evidence of impairment); auditory sensory sensitivity; tasks requiring speech/audio comprehension. Risks: performance decrement in neurotypical users; hearing exposure if volume uncapped. Data used: attention_level (inferred from behaviour); omission_rate (task telemetry). Regulatory notes: Wellness framing only ('may help some people focus'); claims of treating ADHD would move toward medical-device territory. Volume caps advisable for minors. Reward schedule: none. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Background music during tasks (auditory, ambient). User-selected background music (calm, low-salience) available as an optional focus aid. Expected effect: Task performance; minimal effect overall. Evidence (meta-analysis): A small meta-analysis (5 studies) concluded music interventions were minimally effective for increasing task performance in children and adolescents with ADHD. The authors called for better-designed research. Treat as weak/near-null evidence. Contraindications: lyrics during reading/verbal tasks; auditory sensory sensitivity. Risks: distraction; evidence base very small (k=5). Data used: time_on_task_min. Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: none. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Short moderate-intensity movement break (text, notification). Prompted 5–15 min bout of moderate physical activity (walk, active game) between task blocks. Expected effect: Executive function (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility) improvement; chronic programmes show moderate effects (e.g., inhibitory control SMD −0.69 in one 2026 meta-analysis); acute single-session effects positive but smaller. Evidence (meta-analysis): Multiple meta-analyses of RCTs report that physical activity improves executive functions in children with ADHD, with largest effects on inhibitory control and substantial heterogeneity. A three-level meta-analysis specifically examined single exercise sessions, supporting the acute 'break' form. Evidence is mainly from children and chronic programmes; acute break effects are less certain. Contraindications: do not interrupt hyperfocus/productive flow; physical limitations or unsafe environment (e.g., classroom without supervision). Risks: task re-entry cost after break; heterogeneous effect sizes. Data used: time_on_task_min; fatigue (self-report or inferred). Regulatory notes: For minors, push prompts should respect DSA Art. 28 guideline expectations on notifications (e.g., none during sleep hours). Reward schedule: none. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Do-not-suppress movement policy during working-memory tasks (environmental, in-app). System rule: when motion/fidget is detected during working-memory-heavy tasks, do NOT prompt the user to sit still; optionally suggest a fidget tool or standing position. Expected effect: Preserve working-memory performance; in ADHD, higher within-child gross motor activity predicted better WM performance (not normalised); in typically developing children it predicted somewhat lower performance. Evidence (observational): In 29 boys with ADHD and 23 typically developing boys (8–12 y), more gross motor activity predicted significantly better phonological working-memory performance in ADHD but not in controls, and did not change attention. Authors recommend not over-correcting movement during WM-dependent academic tasks. Small, all-male, correlational within-subject design. Contraindications: neurotypical users (movement associated with lower WM performance); unsafe movement contexts. Risks: misclassifying non-compensatory restlessness; small all-male sample limits generalisation. Data used: motion_fidget (accelerometer/camera — biometric/inferred, flag). Regulatory notes: Motion sensing of minors is personal data; under the UK Children's Code, keep profiling/monitoring off by default and inform the child when monitoring is active. Reward schedule: none. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Fixed-interval timed breaks (Pomodoro variant) (visual, in-app). Work/break cycles (e.g., 25/5 or 12/3) with an in-app visual timer; adaptive variant lets the user self-regulate break timing. Expected effect: Fatigue, concentration, motivation; no reliable learning-performance difference vs self-regulated breaks in general students; direction of subjective effects is mixed across studies. Evidence (theory/expert opinion): No controlled trial compares fixed versus self-regulated breaks in people with ADHD. In general university students, a 2023 RCT reported less fatigue and better concentration with systematic breaks, while a 2026 study (N=176) found self-regulated breaks produced better mood with no difference in reading comprehension. The only ADHD-specific Pomodoro study found was a small robot-guided conference paper in 8-year-olds without a self-regulated comparison. Contraindications: do not interrupt hyperfocus; time pressure anxiety from visible countdowns. Risks: fixed interruptions may break productive flow; no ADHD-specific evidence. Data used: time_on_task_min; fatigue (self-report). Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: none. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Periodic self-monitoring prompt ('Was I on task?') (text, notification). At intervals, the app asks the user to self-record whether they were on task; optional self-graphing and self-reinforcement. Expected effect: Increased on-task behaviour and academic productivity/accuracy; combined effect sizes >1.0 (single-case/classroom studies). Evidence (meta-analysis): A meta-analysis of self-regulation interventions (self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement, self-management, self-reinforcement) for children with ADHD reported combined effect sizes above 1.0 for on-task behaviour, inappropriate behaviour, and academic accuracy and productivity. A later meta-analytic review of classroom interventions found self-regulation and consequence-based strategies among the most effective for off-task behaviour. Effects come largely from single-case designs with teacher-supported implementation. Contraindications: do not interrupt hyperfocus; users who find frequent prompts aversive. Risks: prompt fatigue; self-report inaccuracy; single-case evidence may overstate effects. Data used: self-report on-task ratings; gaze_off_task (camera/eye-tracking — biometric, flag) if adaptive. Regulatory notes: Frequent push prompts to minors should be guardian-configurable and quiet during sleep hours per EU DSA Art. 28 minors guidelines; gaze tracking of minors is high-risk data under the UK Children's Code. Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Wearable vibration cue for self-monitoring (haptic, wearable). A wrist/waist wearable vibrates at fixed or variable intervals as a private cue to check and record on-task status. Expected effect: Increased on-task behaviour (single-case: mean ~55% baseline to 70–100% during intervention in one study); student-operated cue outperformed teacher-operated in one thesis. Evidence (observational): Single-case classroom studies pairing self-monitoring with a vibrating MotivAider cue report increased on-task behaviour. A doctoral study found student use of the device produced more time on task than teacher use. Evidence is small-n single-case and partly unpublished; no RCTs located. Contraindications: tactile sensory sensitivity; do not interrupt hyperfocus. Risks: habituation to vibration; stigma if device visible. Data used: timer only (no biometrics) in basic form; optional self-report. Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: none. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Digital daily report card (teacher/parent-assisted) (text, in-app). Teacher rates 2–5 target behaviours daily in-app; parent receives summary and delivers home-based rewards for goals met. Expected effect: Reduced teacher-rated ADHD symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.36, 95% CI 0.12–0.60, I² = 0); larger effects on direct observation (g = 1.05, very high heterogeneity). Evidence (meta-analysis): A meta-analysis of 7 group-design studies (272 children, mean age 7.9) found daily behaviour report cards reduced teacher-rated ADHD symptoms with a small-to-moderate effect and low heterogeneity. A separate meta-analysis of 14 single-case papers (40 cases) also supported the DRC, moderated by study quality and class type. Raters were often not blind. Contraindications: absent or unwilling teacher/parent; punitive use. Risks: teacher burden; privacy of school behaviour data shared across settings. Data used: teacher ratings; parent-delivered reward logs. Regulatory notes: Processes children's behavioural data across school and home; requires a data-protection basis and transparency to the child (UK Children's Code parental-controls and transparency standards). Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Token economy: continuous/immediate reinforcement, gradually thinned (gamified, in-app). Immediate in-app tokens for each completed micro-task, exchangeable for chosen rewards; reinforcement ratio stretched gradually ('stretching the ratio') once behaviour is established. Expected effect: Task completion and on-task behaviour; consequence-based classroom strategies are among the most effective; stretching ratios gave faster acquisition than partial reinforcement with equal persistence. Evidence (meta-analysis): Classroom meta-analytic evidence ranks consequence-based strategies (rewards, response cost) among the most effective for off-task behaviour in ADHD. Experimental work shows children with ADHD learn more slowly under both continuous and partial reinforcement and persist less after partial (20%) reinforcement, while a stretching-ratio schedule produced faster learning than partial reinforcement with equal persistence. A review notes children with ADHD prefer immediate reward and respond to high reinforcement intensity. Contraindications: rewarding speed over accuracy; overjustification risk for intrinsically motivated tasks. Risks: reward dependence; extinction when tokens stop; engagement-maximising drift. Data used: task completion events; keystroke_error_rate. Regulatory notes: Fixed, task-contingent rewards are compatible with EU DSA Art. 28 guidelines if not designed to prolong use; avoid any intermittent/random element for minors. Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Variable-ratio / random rewards (loot-style surprise rewards) (gamified, in-app). Rewards delivered unpredictably after a variable number of completed tasks. Expected effect: Behavioural persistence; in ADHD, persistence after partial reinforcement is reduced (attenuated partial-reinforcement extinction effect), so expected benefit is low or negative. Evidence (RCT): Randomised laboratory experiments show children with ADHD learn more slowly under partial reinforcement and show reduced persistence after it, consistent with dopamine-transfer-deficit theory, although one study found no acquisition deficit at a denser 33% rate. Findings are mixed and come from short lab tasks, not apps. Not recommended as a default mechanism. Contraindications: minors; users with gambling-related or compulsive-use vulnerability. Risks: compulsive engagement; frustration on non-reward; faster extinction in ADHD. Data used: task completion events. Regulatory notes: Direct conflict: EU Commission Article 28(4) DSA guidelines (C/2025/5519) state minors should not be exposed to manipulative design techniques such as intermittent or random rewards. Exclude for minors in simulation. Reward schedule: variable. Minors: no. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Daily streak counter (gamified, in-app). Counts consecutive days of app use/task completion with visual streak badge. Expected effect: Engagement/adherence; no ADHD-specific outcome evidence found. Evidence (none): No peer-reviewed ADHD study of streak mechanics was identified in this review. Streaks are included only so the simulation can model their regulatory exclusion. Loss of a streak may be particularly aversive for users with ADHD-related emotional dysregulation (theoretical). Contraindications: minors; users prone to shame/frustration on missed days. Risks: excessive use; anxiety on streak loss. Data used: daily usage logs. Regulatory notes: EU DSA Art. 28 minors guidelines (14 July 2025) call for features contributing to excessive use, such as streaks, to be disabled by default for minors and for removal of persuasive features aimed predominantly at engagement. Reward schedule: streak_based. Minors: no. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention If-then plan builder (implementation intentions) with task chunking (text, in-app). Before a task, the user writes or selects 'If [cue], then I will [action]' plans and breaks the task into concrete steps; the app surfaces the plan when the cue context occurs. Expected effect: Reduced commission errors/improved response inhibition; children with ADHD reached the inhibition level of controls in one study. Evidence (RCT): In experimental studies, children with ADHD who added an if-then plan to a suppression goal improved Go/No-Go inhibition to the level of non-ADHD children, and combining plans with stimulant medication gave the best inhibition. Evidence is laboratory-based with small samples; task chunking itself was not separately tested. Contraindications: overly complex plan-building flows for young children. Risks: plan-setting burden; lab-to-life transfer unproven. Data used: user-entered plans; commission_rate (task telemetry). Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: none. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Notification batching / silence during focus (environmental, notification). Hold non-urgent notifications during focus sessions and deliver them in batches at breaks. Expected effect: Lower self-reported inattention and hyperactivity symptoms when alerts are off; inattention in turn predicted lower productivity and well-being. Evidence (RCT): A two-week within-subjects field experiment with 221 general-population participants found higher self-reported inattention and hyperactivity when phone alerts were on than when off. The authors explicitly state the findings do not show that notifications cause ADHD or that silencing them treats ADHD. ADHD-diagnosed samples were not tested. Contraindications: safety-critical or caregiver alerts must bypass batching. Risks: missed urgent messages; anxiety about missing notifications. Data used: focus-session state; notification metadata. Regulatory notes: Aligned with EU DSA Art. 28 minors guidelines, which favour disabling push notifications that contribute to excessive use by default. Reward schedule: none. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Virtual body doubling (human or AI co-worker presence) (visual, in-app). Live or AI-simulated co-working presence during a task session. Expected effect: Faster task completion and higher perceived accuracy/sustained attention vs working alone (pilot). Evidence (observational): A small HCI study (12 adults with ADHD) in a VR bricklaying task found faster completion and greater perceived attention with a human or AI body double than alone, with divergent preferences between human and AI. The authors note prior work found no conclusive effectiveness and some discomfort with social presence. Vendor self-report surveys exist but are not peer-reviewed and were excluded. Contraindications: social anxiety or discomfort with being observed; live stranger matching for minors. Risks: privacy of video presence; stranger contact. Data used: session presence; video if live (personal data, flag). Regulatory notes: Live contact with unknown adults conflicts with child-safety expectations (EU DSA Art. 28 guidelines on contact by strangers; UK Children's Code high-privacy defaults); AI companions require disclosure that the user is interacting with AI under the DSA guidelines. Reward schedule: none. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention Brief mindfulness/breathing micro-practice (auditory, in-app). 1–3 minute guided breathing or mindful attention exercise offered at breaks or after errors spike. Expected effect: ADHD symptom reduction for multi-week MBI programmes (children/adolescents SMD −1.30 but I² = 91%); effect of brief in-app micro-practices unknown. Evidence (meta-analysis): Meta-analyses of mindfulness-based interventions report reductions in ADHD symptoms, including a 2026 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs in children/adolescents with a large but highly heterogeneous effect. These are multi-week, often clinician- or group-delivered programmes; brief app-delivered breathing prompts are an untested extrapolation. Earlier meta-analytic work (Cairncross & Miller) covered only 10 studies. Contraindications: do not interrupt hyperfocus; trauma-related distress with interoceptive focus. Risks: low engagement; overclaiming from programme-level evidence. Data used: keystroke_error_rate; self-report. Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: none. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention HRV-triggered paced-breathing prompt (haptic, wearable). Wearable detects low HRV/high arousal and prompts slow paced breathing (~6 breaths/min) with real-time HRV feedback. Expected effect: Emotional well-being/stress in non-ADHD samples; no ADHD-specific attention outcome evidence found. Evidence (none): No ADHD-specific controlled trial of HRV biofeedback was located in this review. RCTs in other populations (e.g., a 5-week HRV-ER trial in younger and older adults) test emotion-regulation effects, not attention in ADHD. Include only as a clearly labelled speculative record. Contraindications: cardiac conditions; anxiety triggered by body monitoring. Risks: false triggers from physical activity; biometric data sensitivity. Data used: hrv_rmssd (biometric, flag); eda (biometric, flag). Regulatory notes: Processing physiological data is special-category (health) data under GDPR/UK GDPR; claims about treating ADHD would risk medical-device classification. Reward schedule: none. Minors: unclear. Claim class: wellness.

Intervention EEG neurofeedback attention training (gamified, wearable). Consumer or clinical EEG headset provides game-based feedback on brain-activity targets. Expected effect: ADHD symptoms: significant only on unblinded ratings (SMD 0.35); no significant improvement on probably-blinded ratings (SMD 0.04, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.18, k=20, n=1214). Evidence (meta-analysis): A 2016 meta-analysis found neurofeedback effects only on ratings by unblinded proximal raters, not on probably-blinded ratings or in sham-controlled trials. An updated meta-analysis by Westwood, Aggensteiner, Cortese, Sonuga-Barke and colleagues for the European ADHD Guidelines Group (JAMA Psychiatry 2025;82(2):118–129; 38 RCTs, 2,472 participants aged 5–40) likewise found no significant improvement in probably-blinded ADHD total symptoms (k = 20; n = 1214; SMD 0.04, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.18). Null evidence for core symptoms. Contraindications: any use framed as ADHD treatment. Risks: cost and time burden without blinded benefit; brain-data sensitivity. Data used: EEG (biometric/neural, flag). Regulatory notes: Therapeutic claims would require medical-device conformity; neural data is highly sensitive health data. Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: no. Claim class: therapeutic.

Intervention Adaptive game-based attention training (AKL-T01 class) (gamified, in-app). Adaptive multitasking video game targeting attentional control, ~25 min/day for 4 weeks. Expected effect: Improved objective attention (TOVA API mean change 0.93 vs 0.03 for control, adjusted p = 0.006) vs digital control; no difference on ADHD-RS symptoms. Evidence (RCT): The STARS-ADHD RCT (348 children aged 8–12, 20 US sites) found AKL-T01 improved an objective attention measure versus a word-game control, but not clinician-rated ADHD-RS symptoms. A broader computerized cognitive training meta-analysis (Westwood et al., Mol Psychiatry 2023; 36 RCTs, 17 of them working-memory training) found, in the 14 trials with probably-blinded data, no effect on ADHD total symptoms (SMD 0.12, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.25) and only a small improvement in inattention (SMD 0.17, 95% CI 0.02–0.31). Trials were industry-sponsored. Contraindications: screen-time limits; framing as ADHD treatment outside a regulated product. Risks: mild treatment-related adverse events in STARS-ADHD: frustration (5/180, 3%) and headache (3/180, 2%); no serious adverse events or discontinuations (Kollins et al. 2020); screen time. Data used: gameplay performance telemetry. Regulatory notes: AKL-T01 (EndeavorRx) is an FDA-cleared prescription digital therapeutic for children 8–12; replicating its therapeutic claims in a simulation-derived product would imply medical-device status. Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: with_guardian_control. Claim class: therapeutic.

Intervention Computerized working-memory training (gamified, in-app). Adaptive span tasks practised daily over several weeks. Expected effect: Improves trained working-memory performance; limited/no effect on blinded ADHD symptoms (probably-blinded ADHD total SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.01–0.40; no effect of WM training specifically on symptoms). Evidence (meta-analysis): A 2015 meta-analysis found cognitive training improved working-memory performance but had limited effects on ADHD symptoms under blinded assessment, with no symptom effect of working-memory training specifically. A 2023 update of 36 RCTs found no effect on probably-blinded ADHD total symptoms. External working-memory aids (lists, reminders) were not evaluated in the sources found. Contraindications: framing as symptom treatment. Risks: time cost without functional transfer. Data used: task performance telemetry. Regulatory notes:  Reward schedule: fixed. Minors: yes. Claim class: wellness.
